variants.name: asyncio write() + await drain() / bounded asyncio.Queue
variants.implementation_notes: Python's default is pull: `for`/`async for` over a generator or async generator asks for one item at a time, so a producer that yields is suspended until the consumer requests the next value and no buffer exists to overflow. For push pipelines asyncio supplies the explicit high-water mark: after writer.write(...) the coroutine awaits writer.drain(), which returns only when the transport buffer is below its low watermark (transport.set_write_buffer_limits sets the pair), and asyncio.Queue(maxsize=n) suspends put() once the queue is full - the event-loop equivalents of a blocking queue. The classic structure of a queue plus threads is therefore replaced by one await, and threads are only needed for blocking libraries.
variants.code_sketch:
async def pump(src, dst):
    async for chunk in src:              # pull: the producer waits for us
        dst.write(chunk)                 # queues in the transport buffer
        await dst.drain()                # returns when the buffer is drained

queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=64)
await queue.put(item)                    # suspends while the consumer is behind
pitfalls: Writing in a loop without awaiting drain() buffers the whole payload in the transport and defeats the high-water mark.
Using asyncio primitives across event loops or threads is unsupported: a queue or semaphore must stay with its event loop; use queue.Queue plus asyncio.to_thread()/run_in_executor across threads.
A synchronous blocking call inside the consumer stalls the loop, so nothing drains and the buffer grows even though the code looks correct.
put_nowait() raising QueueFull is the explicit shed path - swallowing the exception loses work silently.

variants.name: queue.Queue(maxsize) with a blocking put
variants.implementation_notes: In threaded Python the bounded hand-off is queue.Queue(maxsize=n): put() blocks the producer thread while full, get() blocks the consumer while empty, and put(item, block=False)/put_nowait() raise queue.Full as the shed path - so the classic queue-with-lock structure is provided by the standard library and never written by hand. Sizing is Little's law: bound the queue so the backlog cannot exceed consumer_rate x acceptable_latency, and use task_done()/join() to know when the work has actually been processed. concurrent.futures pools give a convenient wrapper, but their work queue is unbounded, so the bound has to be added explicitly.
pitfalls: ThreadPoolExecutor.submit() queues without limit: max_workers bounds threads, not the backlog, so a bounded queue or a semaphore is still required in front.
A daemon consumer that dies leaves the producer blocked in put() forever; shutdown needs a sentinel plus join().
maxsize<=0 means an unbounded queue - the default of queue.Queue() - which is the failure mode the pattern exists to prevent.
Python threads share the GIL, so backpressure bounds memory and latency but does not make CPU-bound stages concurrent.
